article.title: Fantasy Sports Can Teach
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Draft Is Only the Beginning Every fall, fantasy managers spend weeks preparing for a single evening. They study rankings, run mock drafts, and argue over the first pick. Then the season starts, and most of them learn that draft night settles very little. Injuries pile up, bye weeks arrive, and the waiver wire fills with players nobody saw coming. Matthew Bissell, a lifelong football, baseball, and basketball fan who plays in fantasy leagues, recognizes that cycle. As a financial consultant with The Broker Group, he watches families treat a financial plan the way many managers treat the draft: something to finish once and set aside. A plan built at one point in life reflects the information available at that moment. Jobs change, children grow, and priorities shift. For an Oakland financial consultant who works with clients on life insurance and retirement questions, the comparison helps because so many people already get it. A fantasy team needs attention all season. So does a household budget, a retirement account, or a life insurance policy. Building a Roster That Can Absorb an Injury Experienced fantasy players learn to draft depth. A roster built entirely around one star can collapse the week that player goes down, while a roster with dependable backups keeps competing. Families face a similar question with far higher stakes. If a household depends on one or two incomes, the plan has to account for what happens if one of those incomes stops. Life insurance is one tool people use to address that risk, and it works best when it fits the family it protects: the number of dependents, the size of the mortgage or rent, and the years until the children are on their own. The roster comparison also helps people see protection as part of the plan from the start. Fantasy managers don't wait until their starting running back is hurt to look for a replacement. By then, the best options are usually gone. Depth has to be revisited, too. A roster that made sense in September can look thin by November, and coverage chosen before a new baby, a new home, or a career change may no longer fit. A quick review after each major life event keeps the plan matched to the family as it is today. Matthew Bissell on Patience Over Weekly Swings Anyone who has managed a fantasy team knows the temptation to overreact. A player has one bad game and gets dropped, then scores big the following week for someone else. Managers who trade away proven players after a slow start often regret it by midseason. Retirement savings test the same instinct. Market headlines can make a single rough month feel like a crisis, and the urge to pull money out or change course entirely is strong. Steady, long-term retirement planning guidance looks at the full season instead of one bad week: set goals that match a person's age and timeline, contribute consistently, and review the plan on a schedule instead of in moments of worry. Patience comes easier when the plan is clear. A manager who knows why each player is on the roster is less likely to panic. A saver who understands why money sits in a particular account is more likely to leave it there and let time do its work. Read the League Rules Before the Season Starts Every fantasy league has its own scoring system, roster limits, and trade deadlines. Players who skip the rules find out the hard way that their league rewards different things than the rankings they studied. Financial products come with rules too. Life insurance policies have terms, coverage periods, and conditions. Retirement accounts have contribution limits, withdrawal rules, and timelines. Clients don't need to become experts, but they should understand what they own and how it works. A good consultant spends much of the conversation explaining those details in plain language, answering questions, and making sure nothing in the paperwork comes as a surprise later. Matthew Bissell draws here on a career spent in service roles. Before moving into financial consulting in 2025, he worked in community support positions in San Francisco and Oakland, helping people work through practical needs one step at a time. That background shapes how he runs a client meeting: listen first, explain clearly, and give people enough information to make their own decisions. Bringing the Whole Family Into the Conversation Some of the best fantasy leagues are the ones played with family and friends. The trash talk is half the fun, and the season gives people a reason to stay in touch every week. Financial planning can benefit from the same openness. Many households leave money decisions to one person, so a spouse or adult child ends up unsure where things stand if something changes. Talking through the plan together, even briefly, means everyone knows what coverage exists, where retirement savings are held, and what the family is working toward. As a father of two, Bissell knows these conversations come down to one question: whether the people who matter most will be cared for, whatever the season brings. A Plan That Lasts the Whole Season Fantasy football ends in December. A family's financial life has no off-season. The habits that help fantasy managers compete through the playoffs, such as building depth, staying patient, learning the rules, and keeping everyone involved, are the same habits that help families stay prepared over decades. For Matthew Bissell, both teach the same lesson. Preparation matters, but steady attention after the draft is what carries a team, or a household, through the end of the year and well beyond.
